displayQuote: God does not play dice with the universe

meta.title: Who really said "God does not play dice with the universe"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The sentiment is genuinely Einstein's — from a 4 December 1926 letter to Max Born — but he wrote no such sentence. He said 'der Alte' (the Old One), not God, never mentioned the universe, and the popular line compresses two separate clauses.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God does not play dice with the universe'?
meta.ogDescription: Einstein's real 1926 words to Max Born were 'Jedenfalls bin ich überzeugt, daß der Alte nicht würfelt' — the Old One does not throw dice. The famous English one-liner is a compression.

answer.label: The thought is Einstein's — the sentence isn't
answer.sourceLine: Einstein wrote the underlying line to Max Born on 4 December 1926: “Jedenfalls bin ich überzeugt, daß der Alte nicht würfelt” — at any rate, I am convinced that the Old One does not throw dice. He wrote der Alte, not Gott; he did not say ‘with the universe’; and the familiar sentence welds together two clauses that sit apart in the letter.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Born–Einstein Letters, trans. Irene Born (Walker & Co., 1971)

source.excerpt: Die Quantenmechanik ist sehr achtung-gebietend. Aber eine innere Stimme sagt mir, daß das doch nicht der wahre Jakob ist. Die Theorie liefert viel, aber dem Geheimnis des Alten bringt sie uns kaum näher. Jedenfalls bin ich überzeugt, daß der Alte nicht würfelt.
trail: The passage is from Einstein’s letter to Max Born of 4 December 1926, published in The Born–Einstein Letters. Irene Born’s translation runs: ‘Quantum mechanics is certainly imposing… The theory says a lot, but does not really bring us any closer to the secret of the “old one.” I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not throw dice’ German and English side by side ↗.

Einstein’s word is der Alte — ‘the Old One,’ his habitual, half-affectionate name for whatever sets the laws — not Gott. Rendering it ‘God’ imports a theological weight the German does not carry what Einstein meant ↗.

Neither ‘with the universe’ nor the single-sentence structure appears in the letter: the popular line fuses ‘the secret of the Old One’ with ‘does not throw dice’ and adds an object of its own the letters ↗.
source.excerptNote: The closing lines of the 1926 letter. The famous English quotation is a compression of the last two sentences — and swaps ‘the Old One’ for ‘God.’
source.rightsNote: Mixed, and worth care. Einstein died in 1955, so his German original is out of copyright in the EU and UK (life plus 70, expired 1 January 2026). Its US status is genuinely unresolved: the letter was unpublished in 1926 and first published in 1969–71, which under the US rule for previously-unpublished works can extend protection past 2026. Separately, Irene Born’s 1971 English translation carries its own live copyright. Safest course: quote the German with attribution, keep the Born translation to a short cited excerpt, or translate it yourself. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. His long resistance to the probabilistic core of quantum mechanics produced this line in private correspondence with Max Born — part of a decades-long argument Born ultimately felt Einstein lost. Einstein used ‘der Alte’ and similar figures often; he was not describing a personal deity, a point he made repeatedly when readers assumed otherwise.

misattribution.heading: Right thinker, rewritten sentence
misattribution.intro: Nobody is wrong about who thought this — it is Einstein, and the letter is dated and published. What circulates is a tidied English sentence he never wrote, and the tidying changed the meaning in at least two places.

items.why: ‘Der Alte’ is ‘the Old One’ — a wry personification Einstein used for the order behind physical law. Translating it ‘God’ recruits him for a theological claim he spent years disclaiming context ↗.
The letter says only that the Old One does not throw dice. ‘With the universe’ is an English addition that appears nowhere in the German.
The popular quotation fuses the ‘secret of the Old One’ clause with the dice clause. In the letter they are separate sentences making separate points full passage ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Einstein’s conviction, from a documented 1926 letter — but ‘God does not play dice with the universe’ is a paraphrase, not a quotation sourced text ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Einstein was not making a religious statement; he was losing an argument about physics. Quantum mechanics had begun to describe the world in probabilities, and he could not accept that chance sat at the bottom of reality rather than at the limit of our knowledge.

Born kept the letters for forty-five years and published them with his own commentary — which is why one of the most-quoted sentences in science exists only as a compressed English rendering of a private German aside.
detailsBody: German: ‘Jedenfalls bin ich überzeugt, daß der Alte nicht würfelt.’
Literal: ‘At any rate, I am convinced that the Old One does not throw dice.’
Born’s 1971 translation: ‘I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not throw dice.’
Popular form: ‘God does not play dice with the universe’ — three changes from the original.
